1.topic: What science is and the scientific method
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. say what science is and why it matters in daily life;
2. name the steps of the scientific method;
3. carry out a simple fair investigation and say what was kept the same.

## Materials

A candle, matches, a jar, two identical cups, water, a stopwatch, chart paper and markers.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: why does the garri in Mama's kitchen go soft when it is left uncovered in the rainy season? Take answers and write the word 'question' on the board. Tell the class that science starts exactly there.

## Development

1. Science is the careful study of the world around us by observing, testing and finding reasons. Give examples: why iron rusts, why a danfo needs fuel, why harmattan dries the skin.
2. Teach the steps: ask a question, make a guess (hypothesis), test it with an experiment, record what you see, and write a conclusion.
3. Demonstrate a fair test: put a lit candle under a small jar and a large jar and time how long each flame lasts. Show that the jar size is the one thing changed; the candle, the starting time and the table are kept the same.
4. Introduce variables in plain words: the thing you change, the thing you measure, the things you keep the same.
5. Stress safety: long hair tied back, matches kept by the teacher, no running.

## Class activity

In groups of four, learners plan how to find out whether warm water or cold water dissolves sugar faster, and list what they must keep the same.

## Evaluation

1. What is a hypothesis?
2. Why must a test be fair?
3. Name two ways science helps a family in your area.

## Assignment

Write the five steps of the scientific method in your own words and plan a fair test on whether a wet cloth dries faster in sun or in shade. Hand in on the app.

reading.title: Thinking like a scientist
reading.content:
# Thinking like a scientist

## What is science?

Science is the careful study of the world by looking closely, testing ideas and finding reasons for what happens. A farmer who notices that maize planted early grows taller is doing science when he plants two rows on different days and compares them.

## Why science matters

Science gives us clean water, medicines, mobile phones, better seeds and safer roads. When a nurse boils a feeding bottle to kill germs, she is using science.

## The scientific method

Scientists follow steps that help them avoid being fooled:

1. **Ask a question.** Why does bread go mouldy faster in the rainy season?
2. **Make a hypothesis.** This is a sensible guess that can be tested: "Bread goes mouldy faster when the air is damp."
3. **Test it.** Do an experiment.
4. **Record what you see.** Use a table. Write numbers where you can.
5. **Conclude.** Say whether the results support your hypothesis.

## A fair test

A test is fair when you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.

**Worked example.** Ada wants to know whether seeds grow better in sand or in garden soil. She puts 10 beans in a cup of sand and 10 beans in a cup of garden soil. She uses the same size cups, gives each 50 ml of water every day and puts both on the same window. 

- The thing she **changes**: the type of soil.
- The thing she **measures**: how many beans have sprouted after 7 days.
- The things she **keeps the same**: cup size, number of beans, water and place.

If she gave the sand more water, the test would not be fair, because she would not know whether water or soil caused the difference.

## Staying safe

Always listen to your teacher, tie back long hair, never taste anything in the laboratory and wash your hands after the work.

2.topic: Measuring length, mass, volume and time
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name the instrument and SI unit for length, mass, volume and time;
2. read a ruler, a measuring cylinder, a balance and a stopwatch correctly;
3. change between metres and centimetres, and kilograms and grams;
4. find the volume of a stone by displacement of water.

## Materials

Metre rules, tape measure, a kitchen scale or beam balance, measuring cylinders, a stone tied with thread, water, a stopwatch or phone timer.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask two learners to say how long the classroom is without any tool. Then measure with a tape. Discuss why the guesses were different and why we need standard units.

## Development

1. Teach the four quantities with their SI units: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), volume (cubic metre, but litre and millilitre in daily use) and time (second, s).
2. Show how to read a ruler with the eye straight above the mark, starting from zero, and how to read a measuring cylinder at the bottom of the curved surface (meniscus) at eye level.
3. Conversions: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 kg = 1,000 g, 1 litre = 1,000 ml. Work 2.5 m = 250 cm and 3,400 g = 3.4 kg.
4. Demonstrate displacement: 50 ml of water in a cylinder, lower in the stone, read 68 ml. Volume of the stone = 68 − 50 = 18 ml = 18 cm³.
5. Time: show the stopwatch and ask learners to time ten swings of a pendulum thread.

## Class activity

Pairs measure the length of the desk, the mass of a pencil case and the volume of water in a bottle, and record each with its unit in a table.

## Evaluation

1. Which instrument measures mass?
2. Change 450 cm to metres.
3. A stone is lowered into 30 ml of water and the level rises to 42 ml. What is its volume?

## Assignment

Measure five objects at home (a cup, a shoe, a bucket of water, a book, a spoon) and record the quantity, instrument and unit in a table.

reading.title: Measuring things properly
reading.content:
# Measuring things properly

## Why we measure

If you buy cloth from a trader at Balogun market and she says "about this much", you may be cheated. A measurement uses a number and a unit so everybody agrees.

## Four quantities and their units

| Quantity | Instrument | SI unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Length | Ruler, tape measure | metre (m) |
| Mass | Beam balance, scale | kilogram (kg) |
| Volume of a liquid | Measuring cylinder | litre (l), millilitre (ml) |
| Time | Stopwatch, clock | second (s) |

## Reading instruments correctly

- **Ruler:** put the zero mark at the start of the object and look straight down on the mark. Looking from the side gives a wrong reading.
- **Measuring cylinder:** place it on a flat table and read the bottom of the curved surface of the water with your eye level with it.
- **Balance:** make sure the pointer is at zero before you begin.

## Changing units

- 1 m = 100 cm
- 1 km = 1,000 m
- 1 kg = 1,000 g
- 1 litre = 1,000 ml

**Worked example 1.** A rope is 3.2 m long. In centimetres: 3.2 × 100 = 320 cm.

**Worked example 2.** A bag of rice has a mass of 5,000 g. In kilograms: 5,000 ÷ 1,000 = 5 kg.

## Volume of a stone

A stone has no regular shape, so we cannot measure it with a ruler. Pour water into a measuring cylinder and read it. Lower the stone gently on a thread and read again. The rise in water level is the volume of the stone.

**Worked example 3.** The water reads 40 ml before and 55 ml after. Volume of stone = 55 − 40 = 15 ml, which is 15 cm³.

The stone pushes the water out of its place. This is called **displacement**.

3.topic: Solids, liquids and gases, and changes of state
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe the properties of solids, liquids and gases;
2. explain melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation and boiling;
3. use the idea that particles are close or far apart to explain the three states.

## Materials

Ice cubes, a beaker, a hot plate or candle and tripod, a thermometer, a balloon, a sealed plastic bottle with water, a syringe with the end blocked.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Pour water from a cup into a bowl, then ask what shape the water took. Place a stone and a balloon next to it. Ask which keeps its shape and which can be squeezed.

## Development

1. Solids have a fixed shape and volume. Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of the container. Gases have neither and spread to fill the space.
2. Show that a syringe of air can be squeezed, a syringe of water cannot. Link to particles: in solids they are close and fixed, in liquids close but sliding, in gases far apart and moving fast.
3. Changes of state: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation (liquid to gas from the surface), boiling (liquid to gas throughout at the boiling point), condensation (gas to liquid).
4. Melt ice in a beaker and heat until it boils. Record the temperature every minute: ice melts at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C.
5. Everyday examples: wet clothes drying, drops on a cold bottle of soft drink, ice block selling at a roadside.

## Class activity

Learners draw particle pictures of a solid, a liquid and a gas and label each change of state with an arrow.

## Evaluation

1. Why can air be squeezed into a bicycle pump but water cannot?
2. What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
3. Name the change of state when water droplets form on a cold bottle.

## Assignment

Find three places at home where a change of state happens, name the change, and say which direction it goes. Submit on the app.

reading.title: The three states of matter
reading.content:
# The three states of matter

Everything around us that takes up space and has mass is called **matter**. Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas.

## Solids, liquids and gases

| Property | Solid | Liquid | Gas |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | Fixed | Takes the shape of its container | Takes the shape of its container |
| Volume | Fixed | Fixed | Changes to fill the space |
| Can be squeezed? | No | Almost no | Yes |
| Examples | Stone, wood, ice | Water, palm oil, kerosene | Air, cooking gas, steam |

## Why they are different

Matter is made of tiny **particles**. In a solid they are packed tightly and can only vibrate. In a liquid they are close but can slide past each other, so a liquid flows. In a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions, so a gas spreads and can be squeezed.

## Changes of state

Heating or cooling can change the state:

- **Melting:** a solid becomes a liquid. Ice melts at 0 °C.
- **Freezing:** a liquid becomes a solid.
- **Evaporation:** a liquid slowly becomes a gas from the surface at any temperature. Wet clothes dry on the line this way.
- **Boiling:** a liquid becomes a gas all through, at its boiling point. Water boils at 100 °C.
- **Condensation:** a gas becomes a liquid when it cools. Drops form on the outside of a cold bottle of drink because water vapour in the air cools against the bottle.

## Worked example

A seller at the roadside leaves a block of ice in the sun. The ice changes to water (melting) and the puddle slowly disappears (evaporation). When she puts a clean plastic bag over a pot of boiling water, water drops form on the inside of the bag (condensation).

Notice that when a substance changes state it is still the same substance. Ice, water and steam are all water.

reading.content:
# Elements, compounds and mixtures

All the materials around us can be placed in three groups.

## Elements

An **element** is a pure substance that contains only one kind of atom. It cannot be split into anything simpler by chemical means. There are a little over a hundred elements. Gold, iron, copper, oxygen, carbon and sulphur are elements. The gold used by a goldsmith in Kano is an element, and so is the iron in a nail.

## Compounds

A **compound** is a pure substance made when two or more elements are joined together chemically.

- Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
- Common salt is a compound of sodium and chlorine.
- Carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out, is a compound of carbon and oxygen.

A compound looks and behaves very differently from the elements in it. Sodium is a soft metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, yet together they make the salt we put in soup. The elements are always joined in the same fixed amount.

## Mixtures

A **mixture** has two or more substances that are only mixed together. They are not joined. Air (nitrogen, oxygen and other gases), sea water, soil and a pot of jollof rice are mixtures.

In a mixture:

- the amounts of the parts can change. A cup of sweet tea can have one spoon of sugar or three;
- the parts keep their own properties; sand stays sand even when it is mixed with salt;
- the parts can be separated by simple methods such as filtering or using a magnet.

## Comparing compounds and mixtures

| | Compound | Mixture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parts | Joined chemically | Only mixed |
| Amounts | Fixed | Can change |
| Properties | Different from the parts | Same as the parts |
| Separation | Hard; needs a chemical change | Easy; a simple method |

**Worked example.** Iron filings and sulphur powder stirred together form a mixture, and a magnet can pick out the iron. If the same powders are heated strongly, they join to form a black compound which the magnet no longer pulls apart.

reading.content:
# The building blocks of matter

## Atoms

Everything in the world, from a stone to the air in a football, is made of very tiny particles called **atoms**. An atom is the smallest particle of an element. It is so small that millions of them would fit across the full stop at the end of this sentence.

Atoms of the same element are alike. All the atoms in a piece of iron are iron atoms. Atoms of different elements are different from each other.

## Molecules

Sometimes atoms join together. A **molecule** is two or more atoms joined together.

- Oxygen in the air is found as molecules with 2 oxygen atoms joined.
- A water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
- A carbon dioxide molecule has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms.

## Chemical symbols

Scientists all over the world use short names for the elements, called **symbols**. The first letter is always a capital letter. If there is a second letter, it is small.

| Element | Symbol |
| --- | --- |
| Hydrogen | H |
| Oxygen | O |
| Carbon | C |
| Sodium | Na |
| Potassium | K |
| Calcium | Ca |
| Iron | Fe |
| Copper | Cu |
| Gold | Au |

Some symbols come from old names. Iron is Fe from the Latin *ferrum*, and sodium is Na from *natrium*.

## Chemical formulae

A **formula** shows which atoms are in a molecule. The small number written low and to the right tells how many atoms of that element.

- H₂O: 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, 3 atoms altogether.
- CO₂: 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms, 3 atoms altogether.
- O₂: 2 oxygen atoms.

**Worked example.** How many atoms are in the formula for glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆? Add: 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms in one molecule.

If there is no number, it means 1. A big number in front, like 2H₂O, means 2 molecules, so 2 × 3 = 6 atoms.

reading.content:
# How to separate a mixture

The parts of a mixture are not joined together, so they can be separated by simple methods. Which method you pick depends on what the parts are.

## Sieving

Use a sieve when the pieces are different sizes. When mama pours garri through a sieve, the fine garri falls through and the lumps stay behind. Builders also sieve sand to remove stones.

## Filtration

Use filtration to separate a solid that does not dissolve from a liquid. Fold a filter paper into a funnel and pour the mixture through. The solid left on the paper is the **residue**. The clear liquid that drips through is the **filtrate**. A clean cloth can be used in the same way when there is no filter paper, such as when ogi is strained.

## Evaporation

Use evaporation to get a dissolved solid out of a liquid. Heat the solution gently in an evaporating dish. The water turns to vapour and leaves the dish, and the salt is left behind. At the coast, people let the sun evaporate sea water in shallow pans to get salt.

## Distillation

Use distillation when you want the **liquid**, not the solid. The solution is boiled in a flask. The vapour goes into a tube cooled by water (a condenser), where it changes back to a liquid and drips into a clean container. The liquid collected is the **distillate**. Pure water from salt water can be made this way.

## Choosing a method: a worked example

**Problem.** How can you separate a mixture of sand and salt?

1. Add water and stir. The salt dissolves, but the sand does not.
2. Filter. The sand is the residue and the salt solution is the filtrate.
3. Evaporate the filtrate. The water goes and the salt remains.

In this example two methods were used, one after the other.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe the properties of acids and bases;
2. use litmus paper to tell acids from bases;
3. name common acids, bases and salts and their uses;
4. explain why safety rules matter when handling acids and bases.

## Materials

Red and blue litmus paper, lemon juice, vinegar, soap solution, wood ash in water, tap water, an antacid tablet, small cups, labels, gloves.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Give a small drop of lemon juice on a clean spoon to each learner who agrees to taste, and a drop of dissolved soap by smell only. Ask what they notice about lemon: sour. Tell the class that sour things are usually acids.

## Development

1. Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and some can burn the skin. Examples: citric acid in orange and lemon, ethanoic acid in vinegar, hydrochloric acid in the stomach, sulphuric acid in car batteries.
2. Bases feel soapy, taste bitter and turn red litmus blue. Examples: soap, wood ash solution, lime water, milk of magnesia. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali.
3. A neutral substance such as pure water does not change litmus.
4. Test the samples on the table with litmus paper and record in a table: sample, red litmus, blue litmus, acid / base / neutral.
5. A salt forms when an acid and a base react. Common salt is the one in the kitchen, but there are others, such as the alum used to clear muddy water.
6. Uses: antacid tablets (bases) ease heartburn caused by too much acid in the stomach; lime or wood ash is added to acid soils; vinegar keeps pickles from going bad.
7. Safety: never taste or smell laboratory chemicals, wear gloves and goggles, and wash with plenty of water if any spills on the skin.

## Class activity

Groups test five liquids with litmus paper and classify them. Then each group suggests a use for each substance.

## Evaluation

1. How can you tell an acid from a base using litmus paper?
2. Why is an antacid tablet taken for heartburn?
3. Why must we not taste chemicals in the laboratory?

## Assignment

Test three liquids at home with a safe test (lemon, soap, water) using a red cabbage extract or ask your teacher for litmus; record what you find.

reading.title: Acids, bases and salts around us
reading.content:
# Acids, bases and salts around us

## Acids

An **acid** is a substance that tastes sour and turns blue litmus paper red. You already know some acids from food:

- **citric acid** in oranges, lemons and limes;
- **ethanoic acid** in vinegar;
- **lactic acid** in sour milk and in fura de nono.

Stronger acids are dangerous. **Hydrochloric acid** is made in your stomach to digest food, and **sulphuric acid** is found in car batteries. Strong acids can burn skin and eat through cloth and metal.

## Bases

A **base** feels soapy and tastes bitter. It turns red litmus paper blue. Examples are soap, wood ash dissolved in water, lime water and milk of magnesia. A base that dissolves in water is called an **alkali**. Strong alkalis, such as caustic soda used for making soap, also burn the skin.

## Neutral substances

Pure water is neither an acid nor a base. It is **neutral** and does not change the colour of litmus.

## Litmus test

| Substance | Blue litmus | Red litmus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acid | turns red | stays red |
| Base | stays blue | turns blue |
| Neutral | stays blue | stays red |

## Salts

When an acid reacts with a base, they use each other up and make a **salt** and water. This is called neutralisation. Common salt is only one of many salts. Others include alum, used to settle mud in water, and copper sulphate, used to spray cocoa farms.

## Uses in everyday life

- An **antacid** tablet contains a base. It neutralises extra acid in the stomach and eases heartburn.
- Farmers add **lime** or wood ash to acid soil so that crops can grow better.
- Vinegar helps to preserve food because few germs live in strong acid.

## Safety

Never taste or smell chemicals in the laboratory. Wear gloves and goggles, and wash well with water if anything touches your skin.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. list the seven characteristics of living things;
2. use the characteristics to decide whether something is living;
3. explain why a car, fire and a seed need careful thought.

## Materials

A potted plant, a stone, a live snail or an ant colony in a clear container, a toy car, a bean seed, a candle, magnifying glasses, a chart of the seven characteristics.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Place a stone, a potted plant and a toy car on a table. Ask learners to say which is alive and how they know. Write their reasons on the board. Return to the list at the end.

## Development

1. Living things carry out seven life processes: movement, respiration (releasing energy from food), sensitivity (responding to changes), growth, reproduction, excretion (getting rid of waste) and nutrition (taking in food). A memory aid is MRS GREN.
2. Explain each with an example. Plants move by bending towards light; they respire all the time; they respond to light and touch; they grow taller; they reproduce by seeds; they excrete oxygen and water vapour; they make their own food by photosynthesis.
3. Show that a snail moves, feeds on a leaf, produces waste and responds when touched.
4. Test difficult cases against all seven: a car moves and uses fuel but does not grow, reproduce or respond; fire grows and needs air but does not reproduce or excrete; a dry seed seems still but is alive and can grow when it gets water.
5. Conclude that something is living only if it carries out all seven.

## Class activity

Learners complete a table that tests ten things (dog, tree, car, fire, seed, river, stone, mushroom, robot toy, bird) against the seven characteristics.

## Evaluation

1. Which characteristic do all living things need to release energy?
2. Why is a car not a living thing?
3. How do plants respond to light?

## Assignment

Observe a plant and an insect at home for a few days and write down which of the seven characteristics you saw.

reading.content:
# What makes something alive?

Look around you: a goat, a mango tree, a stone, a motorcycle. We know that the goat and the tree are living, and the stone and the motorcycle are not. But how do we know? Scientists use a list of seven things that living things do.

## The seven characteristics of living things

1. **Movement.** Animals move from place to place. Plants move too, but slowly. A sunflower turns its head towards the sun.
2. **Respiration.** All living things release energy from food. Animals and plants do this all the time, even when they are asleep.
3. **Sensitivity.** Living things notice changes around them and respond. A hen runs away from danger. The leaves of the touch-me-not plant fold up when touched.
4. **Growth.** Living things grow bigger and change. A tadpole becomes a frog and a seedling becomes a tree.
5. **Reproduction.** Living things make more of their own kind. A hen lays eggs; a yam produces new tubers.
6. **Excretion.** Living things get rid of waste made inside their bodies, such as urine and carbon dioxide.
7. **Nutrition.** Living things take in food. Animals eat other living things, and green plants make food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.

The first letters spell **MRS GREN**.

## Testing things that are not clear

Some things look alive but are not.

- **A car** moves, uses fuel and gives out smoke, but it does not grow, respond on its own or reproduce.
- **Fire** needs air, spreads and seems to grow, but it does not reproduce or excrete.
- **A dry bean seed** does not seem to do anything, but inside it is alive. When it gets water it respires, grows and sprouts.

## A rule to remember

Something is living only if it carries out **all seven** life processes. A thing that does only some of them, like a car, is non-living.

**Worked example.** Is a river living? It moves, but it does not respire, grow, reproduce or feed. So it is non-living.

reading.content:
# The cell: the building block of life

## What is a cell?

A **cell** is the smallest unit of a living thing that can carry out the work of life. A house is built from blocks; a living body is built from cells. Most cells are too small to see with the eye, and we look at them with a **microscope**.

Some living things have only one cell, such as the amoeba found in pond water. Others have many cells. A grown person has trillions.

## Parts of a cell

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Cell membrane | A thin skin that controls what enters and leaves the cell |
| Cytoplasm | Jelly-like liquid where the cell's chemical reactions happen |
| Nucleus | Controls everything the cell does |
| Cell wall (plants only) | A strong outer layer that gives support and shape |
| Vacuole | A space that holds water and dissolved sugars; large in plant cells |
| Chloroplasts (plants only) | Green parts that trap sunlight to make food |

## Plant cells and animal cells

Both have a membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. But **plant cells** also have a cell wall, a large vacuole and (in the green parts) chloroplasts. **Animal cells** do not have these. This is why plants can stand upright without bones, and why leaves are green.

## Seeing cells

If you peel the thin skin off an onion, place it on a slide and look through a microscope, you will see many box-like cells joined together. You can see the cell wall around each one and a small dot, the nucleus.

## Worked example

Why does a leaf cell have more chloroplasts than a root cell? A leaf is in the sunlight and makes food by photosynthesis, so it needs the chloroplasts. A root is under the soil, where there is no light, so it does not have them.
